A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MolLangBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including rendered figures, tables and task equations, support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations on molecular recognition, editing and generation, together with prompt-sensitivity, repeated-run and OCR-validation results.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds model comparisons, property-prediction experiments, complex-substructure evaluations and error analyses.

M1.justification: The three task mappings and the core and extended annotation pipelines remain unchanged. Added model architectures, representations and prompting comparisons are benchmark evaluations, without a newly proposed model or algorithm.

E1.justification: v3 adds BBBP and BACE property-classification tasks and five complex-substructure recognition tasks: alpha-amino acid, glucose-like pyranose, penam, phthalimide and steroid motifs (Appendices A.13 and A.15). These substantially expand task requirements beyond the retained original benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-Max, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-Opus-4.1, plus HIGHT for recognition and Llamole for editing/generation. ChemDFM, ChemLLM and Galactica also gain reported recognition and generation comparisons beyond their v2 editing comparison. o4-mini remains evaluated in the appendices despite its replacement by Gemini in the main tables.

E3.justification: v3 adds Tanimoto similarity, pass@3/pass@5 evaluation and direct-versus-structure-first property-prediction prompts. New SELFIES, chemistry-specific-model and HIGHT recognition evaluations omit atom-index-dependent subtasks and localization accuracy (Appendices A.10–A.16). These introduce substantial additional evaluation protocols; the original core-set sizes and zero-shot evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine chemical-space coverage through t-SNE, structural complexity, SELFIES sensitivity, multiple-attempt success and the downstream effect of structural prompting. Table 3 and Figures S7–S8 add a six-category error analysis and illustrated o3 failures. Existing prompt-sensitivity, OCR-agreement, tokenization and image-generation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new property-prediction experiment explicitly reports three runs per model–task–prompt configuration and mean ± standard deviation (Table S8). Existing o3 analyses still specify five runs; no increase in that run count is established. Revised means and standard deviations are result changes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new models, representations, metrics and analyses; Gemini-2.5-Pro, for example, ties GPT-5 at 0.430 core-generation accuracy. GPT-5's headline scores remain unchanged. The reported five-run o3 editing/generation mean accuracies change from 0.774/0.286 in v2 Table S5 to 0.754/0.246 in v3 Table S10 without an explanation. SELFIES and multiple-attempt results represent additional settings, not changes in the original SMILES pass@1 performance.

T1.justification: Section 2 retains the same mathematical task formulations. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations appear. The standard pass@k explanation and SELFIES illustrations document evaluation and representation behavior rather than new formal results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contribution: a precise, unambiguous benchmark for molecular recognition, editing and generation across representations. The headline GPT-5 accuracies of 86.2%, 85.5% and 43.0% and the central claim that current models struggle remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretations of atom-level editing/generation failures, complexity-dependent localization difficulties, graph–language alignment limitations and SELFIES weaknesses. It also interprets structural prompting as beneficial for downstream prediction and argues for dataset representativeness from chemical-space coverage. The original annotation-cost limitation and tokenization hypothesis remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents snapshots and API providers for added models, further curation and validation details, LLM assistance with annotation wording, and a dataset contamination canary. These improve procedural disclosure without establishing changes to the retained annotation pipeline. The code and dataset links already appeared in v2.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SELFIES, MoleculeNet, fingerprints, HIGHT, Llamole, additional LLMs and contamination prevention. Related work more explicitly discusses structural grounding and graph–language alignment, while retaining the original positioning relative to molecule-description datasets and specialized chemical models.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites related work, separates recognition and editing/generation discussions, reorders existing appendix sections and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Author affiliations and conference headers also change. The introduction, task formulations, annotation instructions and conclusion remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the error-count table, chemical-space and SELFIES figures, and extensive failure-case panels. Results tables expand and reorganize to accommodate models, similarity scores and pass@k metrics; the ranking plot gains models and a revised axis. Existing benchmark examples are retained but redistributed and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential breadth and diagnostic value: it addresses v2's untested graph modality, broadens model comparisons and quantifies failures previously discussed mainly qualitatively. Complex-substructure and downstream-prompting experiments further test the benchmark's motivation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unexplained revisions to o3's five-run summaries and the new claim that Gemini has the highest generation validity, contradicted by Claude's higher value in Table S5.
